proofs.proof_tex:
Apply \texttt{thm:parameterized-late-ramp-frontier} to the specialization certified by \texttt{prop:late-ramp-membership}, with
\[
 c=a_\star=\frac12,
 \qquad
 \delta=\frac14,
 \qquad
 \alpha=0.05.
\]
The diameter threshold and common-void limiting mass become
\[
 \delta(1-a_\star)=\frac18,
 \qquad
 a_\star^c=\left(\frac12\right)^{1/2}=\sqrt{\frac12}.
\]
The theorem therefore gives, for each \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\),
\[
 \liminf_n\Pr_\sigma\!\left\{\operatorname{diam}(D_n)\ge\frac18\right\}
 \ge\sqrt{\frac12}-2(0.05)
 =\sqrt{\frac12}-0.1
 =0.6071067811865475\ldots .
\]
As an exact smallest-instance stress test, if \(m_n=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), direct summation of the target separation and direct multiplication of the late-void probabilities give
\[
 (\tau_1^+-\tau_1^-,\tau_2^+-\tau_2^-,
   \tau_3^+-\tau_3^-,\tau_4^+-\tau_4^-)
 =\left(\frac12,\frac14,\frac29,\frac3{16}\right)
\]
and
\[
 \left(
 \prod_{t=m_1+1}^{1}\left(1-\frac1{2t}\right),
 \ldots,
 \prod_{t=m_4+1}^{4}\left(1-\frac1{2t}\right)
 \right)
 =\left(\frac12,\frac34,\frac58,\frac{35}{48}\right).
\]
Every displayed finite target separation is at least \(1/8\), and the void probabilities agree with the product used in the general proof. The argument is an information bound for arbitrary complete-log confidence sets and is independent of every HT or AIPW limit law.

In \texttt{def:parameterized-late-ramp-family}, specialize
\[
 c=\frac12,
 \qquad
 a_\star=a_0=\frac12,
 \qquad
 \delta=\delta_0=\frac14.
\]
The compatibility conditions become \(M\ge\delta_0\), \(\rho\ge c\), \(K\ge c\), and \(L_r\ge\delta_0/(1-a_0)\), exactly as imposed by \texttt{def:late-ramp-pair}. All potential outcomes, regressions, propensities, intensity and residual profiles, and complete logs in the two definitions then coincide. Proposition \texttt{prop:parameterized-late-ramp-membership} therefore proves every asserted fixed-outcome, boundedness, predictability, profile-membership, and profile-contract conclusion. Its finite-sample separation specializes to
\[
 \tau_n^+-\tau_n^-
 \ge\delta_0(1-a_0)
 =\frac14\left(1-\frac12\right)
 =\frac18.
\]
Thus the exact pair retains the original membership and separation certificate unchanged.

added_lemmas.statement:
For each \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\), the parameterized late-ramp family satisfies the declared fixed-outcome, boundedness, predictable-randomization, intensity-profile, residual-profile, and profile-contract conditions for all sufficiently large \(n\). In particular, \(\bar q^\sigma\in\mathcal Q\), \(r^\sigma\in\mathcal R\), the two profile discrepancies are identically zero, \(G_n=\Omega\) eventually, and
\[
 \tau_n^+-\tau_n^-\ge \delta(1-a_\star)
\]
for every \(n\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\). By \texttt{def:parameterized-late-ramp-family}, the potential outcomes and regressions are the deterministic arrays
\[
 Y_{nt}^\sigma(0)=0,
 \qquad
 Y_{nt}^\sigma(1)=\sigma\delta\frac{(t/n-a_\star)_+}{1-a_\star},
 \qquad
 m_{nt}(0)=m_{nt}(1)=0.
\]
They are fixed under the randomization law, which verifies the condition stated in \texttt{ass:fixed-outcomes}. Since \(0\le (t/n-a_\star)_+/(1-a_\star)\le1\) and \(0<\delta\le M\),
\[
 |Y_{nt}^\sigma(0)|=0,
 \qquad
 |Y_{nt}^\sigma(1)|\le\delta\le M.
\]
Thus the boundedness condition in \texttt{ass:bounded-outcomes} holds. The zero regression is \(\mathcal F_{n,t-1}\)-measurable and obeys \(|m_{nt}(a)|=0\le M_m\), using the declared type \(M_m\ge0\); this verifies \texttt{ass:predictable-regression} and \texttt{ass:bounded-regression}.

The definition of the sequential design gives
\[
 \Pr_\sigma(A_{nt}=1\mid\mathcal F_{n,t-1})=e_{nt}=\frac ct.
\]
This is the conditional law in \texttt{ass:adaptive-assignment-law}. Since \(t\ge1\), \(c\in(0,1)\), and \(c\le\rho<1\),
\[
 0<e_{nt}=\frac ct\le c\le\rho<1,
\]
which verifies \texttt{ass:propensity-range}; the complementary probability \(1-c/t\) is also strictly positive.

For all \(u,v\in[0,1]\), the constant intensity profile satisfies
\[
 \bar q^\sigma(0)=c,
 \qquad
 \frac c2\le \bar q^\sigma(u)=c\le K,
 \qquad
 |\bar q^\sigma(u)-\bar q^\sigma(v)|=0\le L_q|u-v|.
\]
These are precisely the three conditions in \texttt{def:intensity-class}, so \(\bar q^\sigma\in\mathcal Q\). The positive-part map is one-Lipschitz. Moreover, \(B=M+M_m\ge M\ge\delta\), and the compatibility restriction gives \(L_r\ge\delta/(1-a_\star)\). Therefore
\[
 |r^\sigma(u)|\le\delta\le B,
 \qquad
 |r^\sigma(u)-r^\sigma(v)|
 \le \frac{\delta}{1-a_\star}|u-v|
 \le L_r|u-v|.
\]
By \texttt{def:residual-class}, \(r^\sigma\in\mathcal R\).

It remains to verify the profile contract rather than use it as a premise. From \(r_{nt}(1)=Y_{nt}^\sigma(1)-m_{nt}(1)\) and the displayed construction,
\[
 |t e_{nt}-\bar q^\sigma(t/n)|=|c-c|=0,
 \qquad
 |r_{nt}(1)-r^\sigma(t/n)|=0
\]
for every \(n,t\). Because \(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\) and \(a_\star>0\), there is \(N_0\) such that \(\varepsilon_n<a_\star\) whenever \(n\ge N_0\). If \(n\ge N_0\) and \(t<\lceil n\varepsilon_n\rceil\), then
\[
 \frac tn\le \frac{\lceil n\varepsilon_n\rceil-1}{n}<\varepsilon_n<a_\star.
\]
Hence \(r_{nt}(1)=0\), every summand in \(S_{n,\mathrm{rare}}^{\mathrm{early}}\) from \texttt{def:good-event} is zero, and
\[
 S_{n,\mathrm{rare}}^{\mathrm{early}}=0,
 \qquad
 \left\langle S_{n,\mathrm{rare}}^{\mathrm{early}}\right\rangle=0\le v_{0,n}.
\]
The declared types give \(\delta_{q,n},\delta_{r,n},v_{0,n},\kappa_n\ge0\). Thus all three events in \texttt{def:good-event} occur surely for \(n\ge N_0\), so
\[
 G_n=\Omega,
 \qquad
 \Pr_\sigma(G_n)=1\ge1-\kappa_n.
\]
This proves the eventual profile-contract condition in \texttt{ass:profile-contract}, while also proving the stronger asserted exact discrepancy and early-variation conclusions.

Finally, the definition of the finite-population causal estimand and the two signs give
\[
 \Delta_n:=\tau_n^+-\tau_n^-
 =\frac{2\delta}{1-a_\star}\frac1n
   \sum_{t=1}^n(t/n-a_\star)_+.
\]
The function \(f(u)=(u-a_\star)_+\) is nondecreasing. On each interval \(((t-1)/n,t/n]\), \(f(u)\le f(t/n)\); hence its right Riemann sum satisfies
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n f(t/n)
 \ge \int_0^1 f(u)\,du
 =\int_{a_\star}^1(u-a_\star)\,du
 =\frac{(1-a_\star)^2}{2}.
\]
Substitution yields
\[
 \Delta_n\ge
 \frac{2\delta}{1-a_\star}\frac{(1-a_\star)^2}{2}
 =\delta(1-a_\star),
\]
which proves the causal separation and completes the membership certificate.

added_lemmas.statement:
Fix a member of the parameterized late-ramp family and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). For every possibly randomized confidence set \(D_n=D_n(O_n,U)\), where \(U\) is independent of the experiment and has the same law under both signs, if
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\min_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}}
 \Pr_\sigma\{\tau_n^\sigma\in D_n\}\ge1-\alpha,
\]
then, for each \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\),
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\Pr_\sigma\!\left\{
 \operatorname{diam}(D_n)\ge\delta(1-a_\star)\right\}
 \ge a_\star^c-2\alpha.
\]
The bound is nontrivial when \(a_\star^c>2\alpha\). It is an all-confidence-set information bound for the complete logged experiment and does not use a Horvitz--Thompson or AIPW distributional limit.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Put \(m_n=\lfloor a_\star n\rfloor\) and define the late-arm void event
\[
 V_n=\bigcap_{t=m_n+1}^{n}\{A_{nt}=0\}.
\]
By \texttt{def:parameterized-late-ramp-family}, the conditional treatment probability is the deterministic number \(c/t\). Repeated conditioning therefore gives, under either sign,
\[
 \eta_n:=\Pr_\sigma(V_n)
 =\prod_{t=m_n+1}^{n}\left(1-\frac ct\right).
\]
Indeed, if \(V_{n,s}=\bigcap_{t=m_n+1}^{s}\{A_{nt}=0\}\), then \(V_{n,s-1}\in\mathcal F_{n,s-1}\), and \texttt{ass:adaptive-assignment-law} gives
\[
 \Pr_\sigma(V_{n,s})
 =\mathbb E_\sigma\!\left[
  \mathbf 1_{V_{n,s-1}}
  \Pr_\sigma(A_{ns}=0\mid\mathcal F_{n,s-1})
 \right]
 =\left(1-\frac cs\right)\Pr_\sigma(V_{n,s-1}).
\]
Iteration proves the product formula. Positivity follows from \(0<c<1\) and \(t\ge1\).

We next evaluate its limit. For \(0\le x<1\), direct integration gives
\[
 0\le -\log(1-x)-x
 =\int_0^x\frac{s}{1-s}\,ds
 \le \frac{x^2}{2(1-x)}.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(n\), \(m_n\ge1\), and application with \(x=c/t\) gives
\[
 \left|\log\eta_n+c\sum_{t=m_n+1}^{n}\frac1t\right|
 \le \frac{c^2}{2(1-c/(m_n+1))}
      \sum_{t=m_n+1}^{n}\frac1{t^2}.
\]
Since \(m_n/n\to a_\star>0\), the right-hand side is \(O(n^{-1})\). Monotonicity of \(x\mapsto x^{-1}\) yields
\[
 \log\!\left(\frac{n+1}{m_n+1}\right)
 \le \sum_{t=m_n+1}^{n}\frac1t
 \le \log\!\left(\frac n{m_n}\right),
\]
and both outer terms converge to \(\log(1/a_\star)\). Consequently,
\[
 \log\eta_n\longrightarrow-c\log(1/a_\star)=c\log a_\star,
 \qquad
 \eta_n\longrightarrow a_\star^c.
\]

We now show that restriction to \(V_n\) gives a common subprobability component of the two complete experiments. The deterministic conditional assignment probabilities imply, by the same conditioning induction, that the assignment vector has the same law under both signs. If \(t\le m_n\), then \(t/n\le a_\star\), and hence \(Y_{nt}^+(1)=Y_{nt}^-(1)=0\). If \(t>m_n\), the event \(V_n\) forces \(A_{nt}=0\), so the observed outcome is \(Y_{nt}^\sigma(0)=0\) under either sign. The propensity and regression logs are the same deterministic arrays under both signs. Thus, for every measurable set \(H\),
\[
 \Pr_+\{(O_n,U)\in H,\,V_n\}
 =\Pr_-\{(O_n,U)\in H,\,V_n\}
 =:\nu_n(H).
\]
Independence and the common law of \(U\) preserve this equality when the confidence set is randomized. The common subprobability measure has mass \(\nu_n(\Omega)=\eta_n\) and is dominated by each sign-specific law.

Define
\[
 E_{\sigma,n}=\{\tau_n^\sigma\in D_n(O_n,U)\},
 \qquad
 \gamma_n=\max_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}}
             \Pr_\sigma(E_{\sigma,n}^{c}).
\]
The honesty premise implies \(\limsup_n\gamma_n\le\alpha\). Since \(\nu_n\) is the restriction of either sign-specific law to \(V_n\),
\[
 \nu_n(E_{\sigma,n}^{c})
 \le \Pr_\sigma(E_{\sigma,n}^{c})
 \le\gamma_n.
\]
The union bound under \(\nu_n\) gives
\[
 \nu_n(E_{+,n}\cap E_{-,n})
 \ge\eta_n-2\gamma_n.
\]
On this intersection the same set \(D_n(O_n,U)\) contains both causal estimands. Proposition \texttt{prop:parameterized-late-ramp-membership} gives their finite-sample separation, so
\[
 \operatorname{diam}(D_n)
 \ge|\tau_n^+-\tau_n^-|
 \ge\delta(1-a_\star).
\]
Dominance of \(\nu_n\) by either experimental law therefore implies, for each sign,
\[
 \Pr_\sigma\!\left\{\operatorname{diam}(D_n)
       \ge\delta(1-a_\star)\right\}
 \ge\eta_n-2\gamma_n.
\]
Taking lower limits, using \(\eta_n\to a_\star^c\), and using \(\limsup_n\gamma_n\le\alpha\), we obtain
\[
 \liminf_n\Pr_\sigma\!\left\{\operatorname{diam}(D_n)
       \ge\delta(1-a_\star)\right\}
 \ge a_\star^c-2\alpha.
\]
The right side is positive exactly in the asserted nontrivial regime. Every step used only the two fixed potential-outcome experiments, their randomization laws, and complete-log measurability; no estimator limit law entered.

added_lemmas.statement:
In Li and Zhao's unit-level finite-population setup, adaptive randomization permits treatment probabilities \(e_t(z)\) that are prespecified functions of the available history \(H_t\), are strictly between zero and one, and sum to one over treatment levels; potential outcomes are fixed under assignment randomness, and the adaptive AIPW regression at time \(t\) is constructed using only \(H_t\). Their AIPW Gaussian conclusion in Theorem 4(ii) requires Condition 3, whose part (ii), in their notation, is
\[
 \lambda_{\min}(V_{\mathrm{aipw}})^{-1}T^{-1}
 \max_{1\le t\le T}\frac{(L_t+M_t)^2}{\underline e_t^2}=o(1),
\]
where \(V_{\mathrm{aipw}}\) is the scaled AIPW covariance, \(\underline e_t\) is the smallest assignment probability at time \(t\), and \(L_t\) and \(M_t\) are the outcome and regression envelopes.

added_lemmas.statement:
Every member of the parameterized late-ramp family lies in the baseline binary finite-population adaptive-design class described by Li and Zhao, but it does not satisfy their Gaussian Condition 3(ii). Consequently, if a sequence of possibly randomized complete-log confidence sets is asymptotically \((1-\alpha)\)-honest uniformly over that larger baseline class, then, for each sign of every compatible late-ramp pair,
\[
 \liminf_n\Pr_\sigma\!\left\{
 \operatorname{diam}(D_n)\ge\delta(1-a_\star)\right\}
 \ge a_\star^c-2\alpha.
\]
This is a converse transfer by subclass inclusion only; it does not extend the positive profile-net calibration theorem beyond this note's structured binary profile subclass.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
The sourced statement \texttt{lem:li-zhao-baseline-adaptive-class} gives the relevant baseline-class requirements. For the binary parameterized ramp, define the two assignment probabilities by
\[
 e_{nt}(1)=\frac ct,
 \qquad
 e_{nt}(0)=1-\frac ct.
\]
They are deterministic, hence prespecified functions of every allowed history. Because \(0<c<1\) and \(t\ge1\), both probabilities are strictly positive and their sum is one. Proposition \texttt{prop:parameterized-late-ramp-membership} proves that the potential outcomes are fixed and bounded and that \(m_{nt}(0)=m_{nt}(1)=0\) is predictable. The causal estimand is the finite-population treatment contrast. Thus every such array belongs to Li and Zhao's baseline binary adaptive class.

We next verify failure of the additional Gaussian premise. In Li and Zhao's vector AIPW covariance, the control residual is identically zero, so the control row and column are zero and \(\lambda_{\min}(V_{\mathrm{aipw}})=0\). Hence Condition 3(ii), which requires the displayed inverse-eigenvalue expression to be \(o(1)\), is not satisfied. This is not merely an artifact of retaining the zero control coordinate. For the scalar treated-minus-control contrast, let \(W_n\) denote the corresponding scaled AIPW variance. Direct substitution of the deterministic residuals and \(e_{nt}(1)=c/t\) gives
\[
 W_n
 =\frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n
   \left\{r^\sigma(t/n)\right\}^2
   \left(\frac{t}{c}-1\right).
\]
Writing \(u_t=t/n\), division by \(n\) yields
\[
 \frac{W_n}{n}
 =\frac{\delta^2}{c(1-a_\star)^2}
   \frac1n\sum_{t=1}^n u_t(u_t-a_\star)_+^2
 -\frac{\delta^2}{(1-a_\star)^2}
   \frac1{n^2}\sum_{t=1}^n(u_t-a_\star)_+^2.
\]
The first sum is a Riemann sum and the second term is bounded in absolute value by \(\delta^2/n\). Therefore
\[
 \frac{W_n}{n}
 \longrightarrow
 w_\star
 :=\frac{\delta^2}{c(1-a_\star)^2}
   \int_{a_\star}^1u(u-a_\star)^2\,du
 =\frac{\delta^2(a_\star+3)(1-a_\star)}{12c}>0.
\]
At \(t=n\), the outcome envelope is \(L_n=\delta\), the regression envelope is \(M_n=0\), and, for all sufficiently large \(n\), the smallest binary assignment probability is \(\underline e_n=c/n\). Hence the scalar analogue of the Condition 3(ii) negligible-maximum ratio obeys
\[
 \liminf_n
 W_n^{-1}n^{-1}\max_{1\le t\le n}
 \frac{(L_t+M_t)^2}{\underline e_t^2}
 \ge \frac{\delta^2/c^2}{w_\star}
 =\frac{12}{c(a_\star+3)(1-a_\star)}>0.
\]
Thus the late ramp retains a nonnegligible standardized increment and lies outside the Gaussian Condition-3 regime, consistently with \texttt{lem:li-zhao-lindeberg-premise}.

Finally, uniform asymptotic honesty over Li and Zhao's baseline class implies the two-sign honesty premise of \texttt{thm:parameterized-late-ramp-frontier}, because both ramp laws form a subclass of that baseline class. Applying that theorem gives the displayed probability--diameter lower bound. This implication uses only subclass inclusion and therefore makes no assertion that this note's positive calibration theorem holds on the larger class.

prose_updates.tldr: At the critical rare-arm boundary, where cumulative allocation hazard stays bounded, the finite-population AIPW error need not be Gaussian. On this note's structured binary profile subclass, a stopped adaptive-to-Bernoulli-to-Poisson transfer and directed-rational convolution give a computable atom-safe confidence interval with uniform randomization coverage and explicit oracle level and radius slack. Separately, the parameterized late-ramp family with intensity \(c/t\), ramp start \(a_\star\), and amplitude \(\delta\) proves an all-confidence-set frontier: asymptotic \((1-\alpha)\)-honesty on both signs forces diameter at least \(\delta(1-a_\star)\) with limiting probability at least \(a_\star^c-2\alpha\). These witnesses belong to Li and Zhao's larger baseline binary adaptive class but fail their Gaussian Condition 3(ii), so only the converse transfers to that class. The exact \(c=a_\star=1/2\), \(\delta=1/4\), \(\alpha=0.05\) corollary preserves the \(1/8\) diameter and \(0.60710678\) probability, while the declared high-hazard subfamily retains robust radius at most \(0.442M\) apart from certification slack.

project_justification.gap: Li and Zhao's baseline design class permits positive history-dependent adaptive probabilities and their AIPW theorem gives Gaussian inference only under Condition 3; it does not characterize honest-set width when the negligible-maximum condition fails at bounded cumulative hazard. Existing anytime-valid or i.i.d. width results likewise do not calibrate the signed atomic compound-Poisson law or exploit a shared complete-log void event.
project_justification.niche: The bounded-hazard boundary has two linked but distinct phenomena. Structured deterministic profiles make atom-safe positive calibration computationally possible, whereas a parameterized two-sign late ramp creates a common observational subprobability component of limiting mass \(a_\star^c\) on the void event and a causal separation \(\delta(1-a_\star)\), yielding an estimator-free width obstruction.
project_justification.fill: The project supplies a computable finite adaptive-to-Poisson transfer and profile-net interval theorem on the declared structured subclass, together with a parameterized probability--diameter frontier for arbitrary complete-log confidence sets. A sourced subclass-inclusion argument lifts that converse, but not the positive calibration theorem, to Li and Zhao's broader baseline binary adaptive-design class; the exact ramp and high-hazard numerical certificates remain preserved diagnostics.

prose_updates.related_work: Li and Zhao (2026) provide the closest design-based setup: fixed finite-population potential outcomes, positive assignment probabilities that may be arbitrary prespecified functions of history, and predictable AIPW regression. Their Definition 1 and Sections 2.2--2.3 contain the parameterized late ramps as binary special cases, but their Theorem 4(ii) assumes Condition 3; the ramps fail part (ii) because their standardized late increments remain nonnegligible. The present parameterized frontier therefore transfers by subclass inclusion to their baseline class, while the positive profile-net calibration remains confined to this note's structured binary profile subclass. Bibaut and Kallus (2024) organize adaptive inference into martingale-CLT repair, always-valid methods, and direct inversion of nonnormal laws; their review identifies the last route as incomplete beyond special settings. Waudby-Smith et al. (2024) provide exact predictable-logging martingale confidence sequences but do not determine the signed atomic profile radius. Freidling, Zhao, and Gao (2026) condition exact randomization tests on adaptive selection, whereas the present same-log calibration uses deterministic threshold domination. Cho, Bibaut, and Kallus (2025) invert simulated nonnormal adaptive laws under stochastic bandit models; here the inference is finite-population and certification errors are directed outward. Chen et al. (2026) derive a compound-Poisson HT rate law under independent Poisson importance sampling, not a signed adaptive causal contrast with uniform finite-experiment transfer. Hong, Leung, and Li (2020) study limited overlap when effective information diverges, and Shekhar and Ramdas (2023) prove i.i.d. bounded-mean width bounds rather than a common-subprobability frontier for a complete sequential experiment. Barbour and Xia (1999) motivate explicit compound-Poisson error accounting, while Bhattacharjee and Goldstein (2019) identify the generalized Dickman constant-profile reduction. Liberali et al. (2025) remain the applied consumer, conditional on a prespecified expected-endpoint bridge for their GUSTO-1 and EUROPA adaptive-randomization analysis.
